topic: This is a direct follow-up to two prior accepted runs in the reuse directories listed above. Background: on EleutherAI/pythia-1.4b greedy decoding, a linear probe from the last-prompt hidden state predicted the full-continuation sentence embedding with test cosine 0.4283, clearly beating top-k logit-lens token controls (best control 0.181), BUT was beaten by short greedy-rollout controls: embedding the models own next m=3 tokens gave cosine 0.476, and m=5 tokens gave cosine 0.637, both above the probes 0.4283. The likely explanation given in the prior run: the dataset continuations are short, mean about 16 tokens after a sentence-boundary cut, so a 3-5 token rollout already reveals most of the continuations semantics, unfairly favoring the rollout baseline. The reuse directories contain a working reusable pipeline (common.py, build_usable_and_split.py, extract_hidden_and_generations.py, embed_continuations.py, probe_train_generic.py, token_identity_control.py, steering_generic.py, build_summaries.py) plus the original 600-prompt set -- reuse and extend this rather than starting from scratch. Your task: test whether the probe-vs-rollout comparison flips as the target continuation horizon grows. Concretely: (1) generate continuations at multiple target lengths for the same or an expanded prompt set on pythia-1.4b greedy decoding -- at least a short condition comparable to the prior ~16-token mean, plus meaningfully longer conditions such as roughly 50 tokens and roughly 100 tokens (choose exact lengths and how many conditions you can fit in the time/GPU/disk budget, GPU 0 only, keep disk usage conservative as before); (2) for each horizon condition, train the same type of semantic probe (predicting the full continuation embedding from the single early hidden state) and compare it against rollout controls at several rollout lengths (e.g. m=3, m=5, and additionally a couple of larger m values worth testing), not just the same two m values as before; (3) the key output is a clear picture of whether there is a crossover point -- some target horizon beyond which the probe beats all tested rollout controls, since a short rollout necessarily cannot see semantic content past its own length while the probe target is the full continuation; (4) if time allows after establishing the main horizon result, also note as a secondary finding whether a compute-normalized comparison changes the picture (the rollout requires several additional sequential forward passes while the probe is a single extra linear map on top of one forward pass -- is the probe more efficient per unit of recovered semantic signal even at horizons where raw rollout cosine still wins). Produce a report stating clearly, with real numbers per horizon condition, whether a crossover exists, at what horizon, and what this means for the overall hypothesis and its differentiation from Future Lens, ESP, and simple rollout baselines.
progress: Cycle 1 review: ACCEPT - The experiment met the stated success criteria. It produced quantitative results for three horizons (16, 48, 96), reported probe cosine and rollout control cosines for m={3,5,10,20} at each horizon, explicitly computed delta_best_rollout for each horizon, and provided a written conclusion about crossover existence. The protocol also appears faithful to the plan: it reused the prior pythia-1.4b greedy-decoding pipeline, preserved the hidden-state extraction and embedding choices, used a single 96-token generation pass with truncation for nested horizons, kept the fixed split, and saved the requested summary/report/plot artifacts. The main scientific conclusion is clear: no strict crossover versus the best tested rollout occurs up to H=96, though the probe degrades more slowly and the gap narrows substantially with horizon; additionally, the probe already beats the weakest rollout baseline m=3. Since the intended experiment was to determine whether/where crossover occurs, and the result 'no crossover up to 96' is a valid outcome under the success criteria, no further iteration is required for acceptance.
